title: Add/Drop
logline: The weekend before classes, Cal's mail is going somewhere else, the third floor is auditioning, and the one professor who won't let him coast has already read the truest thing he's written.
previously: BROOKS: "Can you swim?" CAL: "Only toward money. Why, is the Rho sinking?"
NORA: "I'm not going to ask you about the motel. That's somebody's life." CAL (a beat later): "No comment."
BROOKS (toasting): "Next time, make it funny at someone else's expense."
BROOKS (on the dock): "Good. Now you know the water."
CAL: "I'll be back in an hour. I promise." PRIYA: "Totally! Go! I'm fine."
Brooks to R.W.: "He came. He swam. You'd have been proud." Read 2:34 AM.
calNow: Cal has told the truth to a blue book and a joke to almost everyone else, and so far the joke is winning. He has said yes to his father's house, to a secret in Margaux's bed and to Priya's 'always', and he can't keep all three. Someone is posting his movements in real time, and he is working very hard not to finish the thought.

cast.name: Dev Okafor
cast.impression: The nicest guy on campus, and the one person who has your back. He covered for your lottery lie twice, nodded when you said you swam, and smiled through Brooks calling his room the charity suite. You chose the Rho dinner over his trip under the school; he handed you a granola bar anyway. He left the building in church shoes and called it a run, and he still hasn't explained the coin or the envelope.

cast.name: Priya Raman
cast.impression: Your self-appointed emergency contact, fast, funny and not eating. When the leak hit, you held her and said it wasn't her fault, and she went slack with relief. At 1 a.m. you heard her in the bathroom with the tap running; she blamed sushi, you promised an hour, and then you stayed away. You told her 'We're ok. Always.'

cast.name: Nora Castellanos
cast.impression: Sharp and fair. She let you buy her coffee, refused to ask you about the motel ('That's somebody's life'), then asked what your father says about the Rho in the fall of '91. You said 'No comment', your father's line. She put her number in your phone, and her follow-up runs Monday. She has her own reasons for being here.

cast.name: Margaux Vance
cast.impression: Marble in daylight, someone else after dark. She ignored you at breakfast, kept your parka, asked once more about your father's schedule, and on the second night asked a question that wasn't on any list ('Who'd you call?'). You kissed her instead of answering. She said your name, fell asleep first, and still says nobody knows.

cast.name: Danny Doyle
cast.role: High-school junior · Busboy at Dot's Diner
cast.impression: A seventeen-year-old busboy with a pencil behind his ear and a side hustle. You bought what he was selling; a stranger at the Rho door recognised his work and called him an artist.

cast.name: Richard Whitaker
cast.impression: Still heard, never seen. He texted 'Wear the jacket' and 'Proud of you', and he hears about you from Brooks within minutes. His private words to you have turned up in another man's mouth.

cast.name: Simon Achterberg
cast.impression: Your self-appointed guardian: a camel-coat poet who diagnoses everyone with a Victorian ailment and caught your lie by watching your hand. You let him adopt you. He is funny and generous, and he watches you a little too closely. You skipped his wine and opinions for Margaux.

cast.name: Yusuf Haddad
cast.impression: Dev's roommate from Dearborn: eleven words a day, all of them devastating. He read the housing PDF and knows there's no lottery. He let it go, and he's already on your side.

cast.name: Brooks Hadley III
cast.role: Junior · Sigma Kappa Rho pledge master
cast.impression: The Rho's pledge master: beautiful, easy, with a laugh you half-recognise and a tell that mirrors your own. He knows things you told only one person and quoted your father's words back to you. He sent you into the dark water and shook when you came back. You get one good insult, he says, and you've spent it.

castNew.name: Tommy Reyes
castNew.impression: A hockey recruit in a towel and one shower shoe, chasing his bag down the stairs, in love twice this week and laughing off something wrong with his eye.

castNew.name: Mae Sato
castNew.impression: The Marlowe's stage manager: headset, clipboard, a deadpan so complete it loops back to funny. 'This isn't an emergency. It's Chekhov.'

castNew.name: Prof. Helen Marsh
castNew.role: English Department · ENGL 210, The Unreliable Narrator
castNew.impression: The English professor who doesn't take freshmen and took you: a voice like a paper cut, and she has already read the truest thing you've written.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD-FLOOR STAIRWELL. DAWN (FRI 08-28, 5:52 A.M.)

Cal Whitaker climbs the last flight of Lowell's stairs in last night's clothes, shoes in one hand, Margaux Vance still on the other one. Bergamot. Graphite. The faint, expensive nothing of her sheets. Gray light comes through the wavy colonial glass and lies on the steps in puddles, and he walks around them like they're cold.
Nobody knows. She said it at 5:50 into the side of his neck, and then she pushed him out the back door past The Fountainhead, still propping it open, still doing its one job.
He left her at four, dressed, the way she asked. He has been walking Alder Falls for an hour because he couldn't face these stairs.
He left her at four, dressed, the way she asked. He has been walking Alder Falls for an hour because he couldn't face these stairs.

His phone is still open to the thing that came in at 3:07. @lowell.three. A photo of these exact stairs lit red by the exit sign, shot low from a doorway, and on the first landing the back of a boy going down. His back. His hand on the banister. Caption: "1:10 a.m.: where's our legacy going? we live here too." Four hundred and twelve hearts. The account has never once been wrong about where he was.
Under it, the texts that came at 3:15, while he was asleep with his face in somebody else's hair.
The dock, the first night. The hour, the last one. Twice now he has looked at her and picked the other door.
The hour. He said one hour, and he meant it, and he didn't come back.
He stops on the landing and types with his thumb before he can make it funny.
Send. He turns the corner onto the third floor.

Priya Raman is asleep sitting up against his door. Her own duvet around her shoulders like a cape somebody lost a war in. Kevin the skull in her lap. The GERALD Post-it stuck to her knee like a name tag at a very sad conference. Her phone face-down on the carpet beside her bare foot. Silver toenails, chipped.
She waited out the hour. And the next four.

The phone buzzes against the floor. His text, arriving, eight feet from where he sent it. She wakes the way people wake on trains, all at once and already embarrassed, turns the phone over, and reads it. Always. Then she looks up at him from the carpet. Bright. Instant. Perfect.
Oh! Hi. That was a long hour.
A beat, in which she decides what kind of scene this is.
I was guarding your door. From Gerald. He's been very aggressive. I think he's in love with you. I told him to get in line.

Cal wakes at 5:52 on the third-floor carpet with a crick in his neck and June's spare blanket over both of them. Priya is asleep sitting up against his door, Kevin in her lap, the GERALD Post-it on her knee. He stayed. He told a girl on Elm Row "not tonight" and stayed on a carpet until the radiator gave up and the windows went gray.
On his phone, the 3:07 post from @lowell.three, which he has decided not to think about before coffee. Under it, the texts she sent at 3:15 from eight inches away.
Her phone buzzes on the carpet between them. She wakes all at once, reads it, and looks at him from close enough to count his eyelashes.
You stayed. Twice.
She touches his face before she says anything, two fingers on his cheekbone, like she's checking he's solid.
You texted me from eight inches away. That's either romantic or a cry for help.
Gerald ticks in the wall like he's waiting to see what Cal does with this.

choices.label: “I'm sorry.” Say it plainly. No bit.

reaction.text: He crouches to her level, knees cracking, and says it with nothing on it. "I'm sorry. I said an hour."
You're allowed a life, Cal. I'm just in it.

She folds the duvet into a square that doesn't need folding. Then, lightly, the way you'd ask about weather: "Was it the horse-sweatshirt person?" He doesn't answer. "Thought so." She pats his cheek like a grandmother at a christening and goes. Her door closes very softly, which is worse than a slam.

"I'm sorry I fell asleep on you." "You fell asleep WITH me. Different preposition." She lets him pull her up by both hands, and holds on one second longer than the pulling needs, and then she's gone down the hall with Kevin under her arm like a football.

choices.label: Blame Simon's: “Lillet. Poetry. A tragedy.”

reaction.text: It comes out smooth and funny, a little bow on it, and his thumb goes to his left eyebrow on the word tragedy. "Fell asleep at Simon's. Lillet. Poetry. Nobody survived."
Simon texted me at two asking if you were dead.

She says it like weather. She gets up, collects Kevin and the duvet and her phone, the whole sad campsite, in one armful. "Cool. Simon's." At her door she touches the frame twice with two fingers, the way she does when she's filing something, and goes in.

"I was at Simon's. Lillet. Poetry. A tragedy." She laughs into the blanket. "You were on this carpet. I have an eyewitness. It's me. I'm the eyewitness." She lets him help her up anyway, and files the joke somewhere he can't see.

choices.label: Say nothing. Carry her to bed, duvet and skull and all.

reaction.text: He doesn't say anything. He scoops her up, duvet and Kevin and all, and she pretends to be asleep and is extremely bad at it. Her eyelids flutter like a silent-film heroine's. Two doors down he lays her on her bed under the fairy lights.
Always, right?
Always.

Her phone is still on the hallway carpet. He goes back for it, and it lights in his hand. Her lock screen is a vertical photo of the two of them on move-in day, his mouth open mid-joke, her face turned toward him instead of the camera. He sets it face-down on her desk, very gently, like it's a sleeping thing, and goes.
Before it goes face-down he sees the notification under the photo: a Health Services request, typed, never sent.

blocks.text: Act One · Forwarding Address
INT. WHITAKER COMMONS, BASEMENT MAILROOM. DAY (FRI 11:10 A.M.)

Under the student center his grandfather built there is a room nobody photographs: low ceiling, humming fluorescent tubes, eight hundred little brass mailboxes with eagle-etched windows, each one a tiny bank vault for a nineteen-year-old's care packages. Behind the grille, a radio plays oldies to nobody. MRS. PELL, sixties, cardigan, glasses on a chain, a townie who has been sorting Whitlock's mail since before its students' parents met, licks her thumb and deals envelopes like cards.
Simon Achterberg is at his own box in the camel coat, reading a slip of paper with the face of a man at a graveside.
"Not for us, but." But. There's always a but. I live in the but. I've bought property in the but.
He kisses the rejection, folds it into his breast pocket next to his heart, and turns to Cal like he's been waiting all morning, because he has.
You thanked me. In writing. At six in the morning. Nobody has ever thanked me for anything; my mother sends a card every birthday that says "Noted." So I've made it official.

From inside the coat he produces a laminated CERTIFICATE OF WARDSHIP. Calligraphy. A gold foil seal from a party store. CALVIN WHITAKER, WARD. SIMON ACHTERBERG, GUARDIAN. CUSTODY: SOLE. VISITATION: SUNDAYS, AND WHENEVER I'M BORED.
Notarized by a girl on my floor who's pre-law and frightening. Laminated at Dot's. They have a machine. Did you know they have a machine?
Cal knows all about the machine. He says nothing about the machine.
You read me on the stairs, so I'm making this official, for my own protection. Sign here. It's laminated. I'm very serious about laminating.
A gift, for your files. A property transfer. Nantucket. Read it in bed; it's better than porn.
Also, I hear I hosted you last night. Was I wonderful? Did I recite?
Priya told him. Of course Priya told him. Cal's lie has been fact-checked before lunch.
Cal opens his box. Inside is one thing: an index card that came by inter-campus mail, red ink, a hand like a row of small knives.

"Mr. Whitaker. I've read your pages. You have been placed in ENGL 210, The Unreliable Narrator. Mondays and Wednesdays, 9 a.m., Pruitt 3. I don't take freshmen. Don't be late; you'll be tempted to. H. Marsh."

"Mr. Whitaker (there is no Pruitt on my roster). You have been placed in ENGL 210, The Unreliable Narrator. Mondays and Wednesdays, 9 a.m., Pruitt 3. I don't take freshmen. Don't be late; you'll be tempted to. H. Marsh."

"Mr. Whitaker. I have your empty blue book. The empty ones are usually the loudest. You have been placed in ENGL 210, The Unreliable Narrator. Mondays and Wednesdays, 9 a.m., Pruitt 3. I don't take freshmen. Don't be late. H. Marsh."

"Mr. Whitaker. I read four charming pages about a swim team. Bring me the real one. ENGL 210, The Unreliable Narrator. Mondays and Wednesdays, 9 a.m., Pruitt 3. I don't take freshmen. Don't be late. H. Marsh."
"Mr. Whitaker. You did not sit placement. You have been placed anyway. Someone should. ENGL 210, The Unreliable Narrator. Mondays and Wednesdays, 9 a.m., Pruitt 3. Don't be late. H. Marsh."
Simon, reading over his shoulder, goes pale with joy, which on Simon looks like consumption.
Marsh doesn't take freshmen. Marsh made a Rhodes Scholar cry in a Volvo. In the parking lot. With the engine running. I'm in that seminar. I'm repeating it.
You failed it?
Not because I failed. Because she let me. There's a difference and it's my whole personality.

That's when Cal sees it: an orange sticker on the inside of his own box door, where you'd only see it if you were looking for something that wasn't there. FORWARD · PERSONAL MAIL TO: WHITAKER LYLE PARTNERS, ONE FEDERAL ST, BOSTON MA.
The typeface is tidy and cheerful and sans-serif. It reads, somehow, like "No worries!"
Mrs. Pell? What's this?

blocks.name: MRS. PELL
blocks.text: Family request, hon. Lots of the legacy families do it. Bills, statements, the bank. Campus mail stays.
Since when?

blocks.name: MRS. PELL
blocks.text: June.
Has anything come?

blocks.name: MRS. PELL
blocks.text: A few things. Went to Boston. Like it says.
Denise's email, Thursday: no mail for you this week! I'll forward anything that comes, as always. He had read "as always" as a figure of speech.
Simon has gone quiet, which Simon never does. The Marvelettes are begging the postman to check and see one more time. Cal's mail has been going to his father's office since before he got here.

choices.label: Cancel the forwarding. Fill out the form right now.

reaction.text: Mrs. Pell slides a pink form under the grille without comment, the way a bartender slides a glass to a man who's decided. He fills it in and signs it Calvin Whitaker, in full, the whole name, pressing hard enough to dent the counter.

reaction.name: MRS. PELL
reaction.text: Effective Monday, hon.
Look at you. Receiving things. Like a person.

It feels like nothing. A pink form and a dented pen. It's the first thing at Whitlock he has taken back from his father, and somewhere in Boston a woman with excellent handwriting will know by tomorrow morning.

choices.label: Leave it. “It's just bills.”

reaction.text: He shuts the little brass door on the sticker. The eagle in the window looks at him. "It's just bills."

Simon watches him say it and, for once in his life, doesn't make a joke. "It's never just bills, darling. Ask my mother." Something goes across his face and leaves again. Then he's off about the certificate's font, which is called Edwardian Script, and how the girl on his floor wanted Comic Sans, and what that tells you about the law.

choices.label: Ask who filed it. Read the actual card.

reaction.text: Mrs. Pell sighs and produces a tin recipe box, the kind with a rooster on it, and walks her fingers through it to W. The card says: "Filed 6/15/26. D. Farrow, on behalf of R. Whitaker (parent). Reason: family preference."
Cal photographs it. The collector again. Then he puts the card back and leaves the forwarding exactly where it is, because it feels important to know a thing before you do anything about it.
You're building a file on your own father. That's my whole personality. You can't have it.
He says it like a joke. His hand is in his coat pocket, holding something, and it stays there.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, DEV'S DOUBLE. DAY (FRI 1:30 P.M.)

Dev Okafor is pre-reading organic chemistry, which no one has assigned yet, with highlighters in four colors and a system nobody else understands. Yellow is "important." Pink is "important to Mom." Green is a secret. Yusuf is on the bottom bunk under the crooked loft with his hood up, laptop on his knees, a man inside a cave inside a hoodie.
Still not level.
It's a design choice.
It's a slope.
Cal is on the floor with his back against Dev's mini-fridge, which hums against his spine like a cat. His phone has been doing things all day. First, NORA:

msgs.text: Is this a threat or a flirt, Castellanos?
You'll know a flirt when I'm wrong about you.

blocks.text: Dev reads it over his shoulder without shame.
She's wrong about you?
She's never wrong about me. That's the problem.
Coffee boy got a courtesy. That's growth, man.
Then BROOKS HADLEY.

msgs.text: You saw the wall. Now learn the names.
You skipped dinner. Learn the names anyway. Your father asked.

blocks.text: And a photo. A typed sheet, the letters faintly uneven, like a real typewriter or somebody who wanted it to look like one. SIGMA KAPPA RHO · FALL 1991 · ACTIVES AND PLEDGE CLASS.

msgs.text: Legacies are quizzed on their father's year. Thursday. Don't embarrass him.

blocks.text: Cal reads it the way he reads everything, fast and then slow. The actives first. "Hadley, Brooks Jr." Brooks's own father.
A face he can picture now, smiling in a top-row oval. Look how happy.
Then, eight lines down: "Vance, Graham."

Vance. A Vance in his father's house, in his father's year. He thinks of a girl at a desk with a smear of graphite down the side of her hand, and he decides, very deliberately, not to think anything else about it.
Then: "Whitaker, Richard C. (Pledge Master)."

Then the pledge class. Nineteen lines, alphabetical. "Abernathy, John." "Brandt, Kurt." "Carver, Paul." And then a line that is only a dash. Then "Cohen, David." Then the alphabet goes on without it, Danforth and Ellery and all the rest, like nothing happened.
Thirty-four names. Thirty-five lines.
Why does a frat have homework.
Why does a frat have a dash.

Cal opens his camera roll. Thursday night, the composite hallway: the empty oval of faded green felt, the brass nameplate pried off, the fragment that's left. T. C. He lays the phone on the floor next to the sheet. Carver. Dash. Cohen. The alphabet has a slot in it exactly the shape of a C.
He hears Brooks in the composite hallway, answering the question Cal asked him: a boy who couldn't swim. Then the laugh.
He has never been inside the Rho. He's never seen their wall. It's just a dash. It just looks like somebody ran out of ink.

Three days ago a reporter leaned across a table at the Grind and asked him about exactly this year. Fall of ninety-one, say. He gave her his father's answer. Now his father's year is sitting on Dev's floor with a hole in it.

choices.label: Forward it to Nora: “You asked about fall '91. No comment.”

msgs.text: You asked about fall '91. No comment.

reaction.text: The dots appear. Disappear. Appear. Dev watches them like a heart monitor.
His own "No comment," turned around and handed back to her with a gift in it. Her "Okay" sounds like a deal she hasn't named yet.

msgs.text: You remembered our deal. Two coffees.
You're getting good at defying people.

reaction.text: He has just done the one thing his father told him never to do, in his father's own words, and he has no idea what he's given her.
Bro.
Bold.

choices.label: Make flashcards. Let Dev quiz you.

reaction.text: Dev turns out to be terrifying with flashcards. He holds them like a dealer and flips them like a man who has memorized the Krebs cycle for fun. Yusuf times them on his phone without being asked.
Cal has all thirty-four names in eleven minutes, his father's year in his mouth like a prayer he didn't choose. Abernathy, Brandt, Carver. "Dash." Cohen.
You say "dash" like it's a guy.
It is a guy.
Nobody laughs. Then everybody does, too loud, the way you laugh in a basement when the lights flicker. Yusuf stops the timer. "Eleven minutes, four seconds." He doesn't say whether that's good.

choices.label: Text Brooks: “Who's the dash?”

reaction.text: Brooks answers in under a minute, which means he was holding the phone.
Then nothing. Dev goes back to green, the secret color. Then, a full minute later, alone on the screen:
Cal reads it three times and cannot decide which father Brooks means.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, STAIRWELL / FOURTH-FLOOR CLOSET ROOM. NIGHT (FRI 10:40 P.M.)

Friday night on Lowell is a sound more than a place: two Bluetooth speakers fighting, a hair dryer, somebody's mother on speakerphone. Cal is coming up the stairs with a Commons sandwich when a hockey bag the size of a body bag comes bouncing down two flights, end over end, and stops against his shins like a dog that wants to be petted.

It is followed, at speed, by TOMMY REYES, 18, freshman hockey recruit out of Worcester: towel, one shower shoe, steam still rising off his shoulders like a racehorse after the fifth at Saratoga. Broad, grinning, a scar through one eyebrow, a face that's always about to tell you something great.
Bag! Bag. Sorry. Hi. It got away from me. It does that. It's got a personality. Its name is also Tommy.

He's locked out. His room is a converted broom closet on the fourth floor whose door locks if you breathe on it, and he breathed on it, and his key is inside, with his phone, his pants, and his dignity.

He talks like a highlight reel. He has been in love twice this week: "A girl in my Spanish placement and a barista at the Grind, both named Danielle, it's a sign, I just don't know what of." He's sending his mother his whole first stipend check for her birthday: "The whole thing. She's gonna yell at me. It's gonna be beautiful."
Wait. WAIT. You're toast guy! "The most Whitaker sentence ever spoken!" I say it to my mirror. I don't even know what it means. I say it before games.
Wait. WAIT. Building guy! Your name's on the building! I eat in your building! Thank you for the waffles!
They pass the third floor. Through Cal's open door Tommy sees the mattress on the floor, then through Dev's the crooked loft. "Bro, who built that, it's like a, it's like a ramp—" "Don't."

On the fourth-floor landing, under a fluorescent tube that's dying in stages, Tommy suddenly presses the heel of his hand into his right eye, hard, and holds it there. Then he laughs. "Light up here's like a dentist." He takes the hand away and he's fine. He's completely fine.

The closet door is old, cut down to fit a doorway that wasn't built for it, and there's a two-inch gap under it. Cal gets down on the floor to look for the key. Inside: a room the size of a parking space. A broom hook still on the wall. A hockey stick for a curtain rod. The key on the bed, glinting, unreachable.
And low in the old wainscot by the bed, at exactly the height of a person lying down, carved small and neat with a knife: B.H. '28 · 4 IN. HOLD. 8 OUT.
Some guy's breathing exercise. Or a bra size. I'm hoping bra size.
blocks.paren: lying on the floor next to him

blocks.text: Cal doesn't laugh. Wednesday, the Quad, a voice like his father's: I lived in a Lowell closet freshman year. Fourth floor. B.H. He knows whose initials these are. He has no idea what the numbers mean. He doesn't tell Tommy.
On the floor inside, Tommy's phone lights up the whole little room. DAD. It rings and rings against the boards. Tommy watches it through the gap and doesn't move a muscle until it stops.
Gimme your phone.
Cal hands it over. Tommy types with his thumb, dripping on the screen, and hands it back: TOMMY (TOWEL).

Captains' practice party tomorrow. The Barn, upper Mill. Bring everybody. Bring the guy in the coat, he scares me in a good way. Now how do I get in my room, because I'm getting cold in a way that feels personal.

choices.label: “Dad's AmEx. Let's see what it can't open.”

reaction.text: Cal takes out the black card his father gave him at fifteen with the words "For emergencies, not for fun," which Cal has always taken as a dare. He slides it into the old latch, jiggles, swears, jiggles. On the second try the latch gives with a sound like a knuckle.
YOUR DAD'S CARD OPENED MY DOOR. I'm naming my first kid Whitaker. Boy or girl. Whitaker Reyes.
The card comes out with a crease across the middle that will never come out. Cal looks at it, bent, his father's name embossed and broken. He finds he doesn't mind at all.

choices.label: “You took a hit today, didn't you?”

reaction.text: Tommy's grin doesn't move. Not even a little. That's how Cal knows.
I'm a hockey player, bro. I take a hit every day. That's the job. That's the whole job description. "Get hit, say thank you."

Then he's back on the bra-size theory, faster, louder, workshopping cup sizes for the fourth floor. June arrives ten minutes later with the master key and a face like a woman reconsidering every choice that led to an RA stipend. Tommy thanks her like she pulled him out of a burning building, and doesn't look at Cal again until his door is shut.

choices.label: Wake the floor: “Lowell Three, we have a naked man.”

reaction.text: Cal leans over the banister and announces it down the stairwell like a ring announcer. Doors open all down the third floor. The third floor comes upstairs.

Priya films vertically from the landing. Tommy, delighted, poses with the hockey bag on his shoulder like a Renaissance statue of a guy who's never read a book. Hunter does calf raises in solidarity. Somebody plays "Chariots of Fire" off a phone.
Priya films the whole thing. She doesn't look at Cal once.
Over the top of her phone she mouths always at him and goes back to filming.
June arrives with the master key and the face of a woman who wanted to be a social worker. By morning the towel is on @lowell.three, and Tommy is thrilled. "I'm basically verified."

blocks.text: INT. KAPPA LAMBDA HOUSE, MARGAUX'S ROOM. NIGHT (FRI 11:30 P.M.)

blocks.song: Hope Is a Dangerous Thing for a Woman Like Me to Have - but I Have It

blocks.text: Margaux Vance at her desk in a St. Anselm's swim parka two sizes too big for her, the sleeves pushed to the elbows. She has kept it four days. She hasn't asked herself why.
Margaux Vance at her desk in a cashmere wrap, shoulders up around her ears.
A sketchbook shut under her left palm like she's keeping it from getting up. On her laptop, the page she has refreshed eleven times tonight: @lowell.three.
The 3:07 post. She has zoomed in on it until the back of his head is pixels. Until it could be anyone. It couldn't be anyone.
The newest post is Lowell's third-floor hallway at three in the morning. She has zoomed in until it's pixels, looking for a door she knows.
Her phone lights. MOM. On the roof, four nights ago, this would have frozen her. She answers on the first ring.
There's an account on his floor. Somebody photographed him leaving his dorm. At one in the morning.

blocks.name: MOM
blocks.text: Leaving to go where?
Silence. Margaux looks at the pixels.

blocks.name: MOM
blocks.text: Oh, Margaux. Good.

blocks.name: MOM
blocks.text: To you? Tell me it was to you.
He walked me home. That's all.

blocks.name: MOM
blocks.text: Then stop walking.
He didn't come. I asked him to, and he sent "not tonight."

blocks.name: MOM
blocks.text: Then go and get him. Be seen getting him.
Margaux closes her eyes.

blocks.name: MOM
blocks.text: Then stop hiding it. Be seen with him. A Vance with a Whitaker is the only headline we can afford this year.

blocks.name: MOM
blocks.text: A week, and you still can't tell me whether his father is coming up for Convocation.

blocks.name: MOM
blocks.text: The navy suit was good. I need more than a suit.
No.

blocks.name: MOM
blocks.text: No, he isn't? Or no, you can't?
No. I won't be seen with him.
A long pause on the line. Long enough for Margaux to hear her mother's kitchen, the good one in Greenwich, the ice machine in the big refrigerator dropping a single cube.

blocks.name: MOM
blocks.text: You don't get to have things that are just yours, darling. We can't afford it.
Click.

Margaux sits there. Then she opens the sketchbook. Whitaker Commons, redrawn in glass: the fake buttresses gone, the stone gone, light going all the way through it like it has nothing to hide. Her pencil finds the steps. She draws one small figure on them, a boy, hands in his pockets, waiting for no one.
Then she erases him. She erases him so hard the paper furs, so hard it nearly tears, until there is only a pale, roughened place on the steps where somebody used to be.

INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD-FLOOR COMMON ROOM, BY THE PRINTER. MORNING (SAT 08-29, 9:30 A.M.)

Marsh's syllabus arrived overnight as a PDF with no greeting. Twelve weeks of books Cal has heard of and four he hasn't. Under week one, a single line in bold, like a slap you could photocopy: Bring to the first class the essay you wish you hadn't written.

He sends it to the floor printer, which Hunter calls the Oracle, because it only works when it wants to and nobody knows what it wants. Today it wants to. It wakes with a groan like Gerald's cousin and begins to speak.

In the tray, under his warm page, there's someone else's job. Six pages of The Seagull, Act Four, every one of Nina's lines highlighted in pink, PRIYA written in the margin with a heart over the i that's been scribbled out. And under those, a title page.
THE BOY ACROSS THE HALL (working title). A solo piece by Priya Raman. Draft 3.
The first line of page one shows through underneath, the way the next card in a deck shows its corner: LIGHTS UP. A hallway in an old dorm. A BOY hides a GIRL in his closet from her MOTHER.
The first line of page one shows through underneath: LIGHTS UP. A hallway in an old dorm. A BOY lets a GIRL read one line of his notebook.
The first line of page one shows through underneath: LIGHTS UP. A hallway in an old dorm. A BOY lets a GIRL read one line of his notebook.
Cal holds very still, the way you hold still when you've walked into a spiderweb and you don't yet know where the spider is.

Wednesday morning he held her while she cried and told her it wasn't her fault, and he felt her go slack in his arms, all at once, like something heavy had been lifted off her back. He'd thought it was grief. He thinks about it now, with her pages in his hand, and it isn't grief he's thinking about.
Since Wednesday she won't stand within arm's length of him. She laughs at his jokes from doorways.
Since Wednesday, since her mother's text, she's been very bright with him and very careful, like a waitress with a full tray.
Down the hall, Priya's door opens. She's singing, "Seagull" or something like it, off-key on purpose. Her slippers slap the floor. She's coming for her printing.
Is Simon's printer broken too?

Ten steps. Nine. Her pages are in his hand.

True. Completely true. She believes him instantly, completely, without a flicker, and that is somehow the worst part of the morning.

For one second her face is pure fear. Nothing performed, nothing for the back row. Then, too loud:
Oh my God, that's about a different boy. Across a different hall. In Edison. His name is Ravi. He's very tall.
She hugs the pages to her chest like a girl in a movie hugging a letter.
Don't read my diary, Whitaker.
She hears what she's said. So does he. Neither of them says anything about it. The Oracle, finished, sighs.

blocks.text: INT. CAL'S SINGLE, LOWELL HOUSE. DAY (SAT 10:10 A.M.)

Before she went back down the hall, Priya turned in her doorway and pointed at him with the rolled-up pages like a conductor. "I'm going to ask you for something later. Be nice to me later." Then the door.

Now Cal is on his mattress, which is still on the floor, staring at his shelf: Winterkill with its broken spine, Kevin the skull, and the cream Rho card propped against both of them like it's paying rent.
His phone buzzes. Twice. MARGAUX (DON'T).
He knows exactly what she means. He also knows whose door he'd have to knock on to make it stop, and it's two doors down, and it has fairy lights.
His phone buzzes. Twice. MARGAUX (DON'T).

Above her new texts there's nothing. The last thing she asked him wasn't a text. It was in her bed at 1:25 Friday morning, her phone face-down for once, her voice smaller than he'd ever heard it: Who'd you call? In the diary. The ice machine. He kissed her instead of answering. She let him. That's still sitting there between them, unanswered, under everything.
She said "not yet" about daylight. He keeps hearing it.
He told her about the call already, in the dark, Friday. She didn't say anything. She held his wrist until she fell asleep.

Dots. Gone. Dots.

blocks.text: INT. FENNIMORE LIBRARY, SPECIAL COLLECTIONS READING ROOM. DAY (SAT 2:00 P.M.)

A hushed oak room on the top floor of the library, the kind of quiet that costs money. A humidity gauge on the wall like a heart monitor for paper. One LIBRARIAN, cardigan and pencil-only rule, confiscates Cal's pen at the door like it's a switchblade.

Margaux is at the long table under the tall windows. White cotton archive gloves. In front of her, laid open under glass weights, the original 1791 plans of Whitlock College, brown ink on vellum gone the color of weak tea. A sketchbook beside them. A pencil behind her ear. No makeup. And glasses: tortoiseshell, a little crooked, the kind you buy because they work and not because they're anything. He has never seen them. He suspects nobody has.
Daylight comes through the tall windows and lands on both of them like a verdict.
This is the light. Yes. Sit down.
On the Kappa back stairs she shoved him off: Not here. Not in the light. This is here. This is the light.
Sit down. Don't say anything about the glasses.
It's the first time they've been alone since the roof.
You picked the poet on Wednesday. Brave.

He sits. She doesn't comfort him about the call. She doesn't say I'm sorry, or that must have been hard, or any of the things girls from Greenwich are trained to say over the phone to a boy whose mother left. She turns a page of vellum with two gloved fingers and says:
Mine would have let it ring.
Then, before he can answer:
Don't tell me the rest. I'll want to keep it.
She doesn't ask a single thing about his father all afternoon. He notices the shape of the not-asking, like a chair taken out of a room.
She starts to ask whether his father is coming for Convocation, and stops in the middle of the word, and doesn't finish it.
Look. They got the chapel wrong.
She shows him: on the vellum the chapel faces the lake, its big rose window looking out over the water. On the Quad it faces the other way.

The plans had it facing the water. They turned it around in 1794 so the trustees wouldn't have to look at the lake during sermons. It made them sad. Rich men hate being sad in public. It's the only thing they're afraid of.
She says it like gossip about people she knows. Maybe she does.
Your father was Rho. Ninety-one. My father's year.
Her pencil stops.
Everyone's father was in everyone's father's class, Cal. That's what a class is.
She smiles, lightly, the docent smile, and her hand doesn't move again until he looks away.

choices.label: “Can I see the sketchbook?”

reaction.text: She looks at him for a long time over the tops of the glasses. Then she opens the sketchbook to one page, only one, and turns it toward him with her gloved hand flat on the corner so he can't turn further.

Whitaker Commons, redrawn in glass. The fake buttresses gone. Light going all the way through the building like it has nothing to hide. His grandfather's name nowhere on it. On the steps there was a figure once. It's been erased so hard the paper has gone soft and furred.
You've seen the hand. Now you get the rest.
Don't make it a thing.
He doesn't. He looks until she closes it, and she lets him look that long.

choices.label: Kiss her in the stacks, in daylight.

reaction.text: She lets him. Against a shelf of eighteenth-century sermons, one gloved hand flat on his jaw, cotton and then not cotton, her glasses knocked crooked and neither of them fixing them.
People read here, Whitaker.
The librarian coughs like a gunshot. Margaux is laughing, the real laugh, the one he's only heard in the dark, into his collar, and then she's pushing him toward the door with both hands.
Go. You've been seen by a librarian. That's enough exposure for one day.

choices.label: “I think I know who runs the account.”

reaction.text: Who?
He doesn't say. He doesn't have to. She reads him the way only she can, and she doesn't like what she reads.
Someone you love. That's worse.
She takes the gloves off one finger at a time, like a woman in an old movie deciding to stay for dinner, except she isn't staying.
Then you have a choice to make. And I'm not in it.
She goes back to the chapel and the water. He's been dismissed. Kindly. It's the kindest anyone has ever been about dismissing him.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD FLOOR, CAL'S DOORWAY. EVENING (SAT 6:30 P.M.)

Dev and Yusuf are at the top of the stairs, dressed for a party. Dev is in a pressed polo, tucked in, with a belt, like a youth pastor on a cruise. Yusuf is in a gray hoodie identical to every other gray hoodie he owns.
This is my going-out hoodie.
Yusuf has never been to a party. Not one. It's a human rights issue. I've written to the UN.

And Priya, in Cal's doorway, leaning on the frame, her Seagull sides rolled up in her fist like a baton. Sleeves pulled down over her hands. Half a Sour Patch Kid in her mouth, which as far as he can tell is dinner. Callbacks for Nina are at eight at the Marlowe, and the reader they've assigned her is a sophomore who reads Chekhov like a GPS. "In four hundred feet, I'm a seagull."
She doesn't say it as a joke, at first. Then she does.
You owe me an hour. I'm collecting. Read Konstantin with me.
You don't owe me anything. You sat on a carpet with me all night. I'm asking anyway. Read Konstantin with me.
And don't tell me you're going to Simon's.
You carried me. You can carry a scene.
Sorry's a down payment. This is the rest.
You've read my pages. Read Chekhov's. His are better. Slightly.
She doesn't mention the pages. She holds the sides very tightly. Her knuckles are white around a Russian.
The dock, the first night. The hour, the last one. And now this.
The hour, the last time. And now this.
Go with her, man. Or come with us. Both are good.
One is better.
Dev looks at Yusuf. Yusuf looks at nothing. Priya looks at Cal, and for once she isn't performing, and that's the hardest look on the floor.

choices.label: “Get your coat, Nina. I'm paying the hour.”

reaction.text: Priya makes a sound like a kettle coming to the boil, a high, helpless, ridiculous sound, and covers her mouth with the sides. Dev grins and salutes. Yusuf nods once, the way a judge nods.
Go. We'll tell Tommy you're doing theater. He'll respect it. He respects everything.

Priya is already gone down the hall for her coat, shouting back over her shoulder that he can't wear that, he looks like a man who sells boats, wear the black, the black sweater, the one with the hole, Konstantin would have a hole. He changes into the black sweater with the hole. He doesn't even argue.

choices.label: “I promised Tommy. I'll come find you after.”

reaction.text: Totally! Go! Obviously!
She's already turning. Three times now, and she says the same three words every time, in the same bright order, like a recording of a girl.
Break a leg. Not literally. Hockey people, they take it literally.
Her door closes. Yusuf looks at it, then at Cal, and doesn't say anything, which from Yusuf is a paragraph.

blocks.text: INT. THE BARN (HOCKEY HOUSE), UPPER MILL STREET. NIGHT (SAT 10:00 P.M.)

The Barn is a sagging Victorian at the top of Mill Street that the hockey team has rented since the Reagan administration. Low ceilings built for shorter centuries. A stuffed bobcat in a Bruins jersey presiding over the stairs. A hockey net in the dining room serving as a beer-pong backstop. A sign on the captain's door, in Sharpie: OUT OF TOWN TILL MONDAY. TOUCH NOTHING. Someone has added: WE TOUCHED EVERYTHING.
Tommy Reyes is king of it, shirtless under a navy blazer with the sleeves shoved up, introducing everyone to everyone like a mayor at a ribbon cutting.
This is Whitaker! His dad's credit card opened my door! I owe this man my pants!
This is Whitaker! The guy who made me famous! Two thousand likes! My mom saw it! She's furious!
Around Cal, Tommy is one degree louder than around anyone else, performing fine, performing great, performing a man who has never taken a hit in his life.

Dev has taken up a position at the kitchen island with a lime seltzer and the air of a man guarding a border. Yusuf stands against the wall beside him like a security camera somebody installed in 1974.
I'm observing.
He's having a great time. Look at him. That's his great-time face.
Simon arrives at 10:15 in the camel coat, in a house full of men in mesh shorts, and pauses on the threshold like a duchess entering a mine.
I came to see how the other half concusses.

Then the Kappas, in a laughing wave with Rho brothers in navy quarter-zips threaded through them, Fitz red-faced at the front with a lacrosse stick he has no reason to own. And in the middle of all of it, Margaux Vance on Brooks Hadley's arm. His hand flat on the small of her back like a man resting his palm on a car he's about to buy. The merger, in public, under a stuffed bobcat.
She does not look at Cal. Not once. She is extremely good at it.
She does not look at Cal. She angles her body, very slightly, so that Brooks is always between them, like a woman standing behind a pillar in a church.
She looks at Cal exactly once, across the room, and there's a beat of the library in it, the glasses and the daylight, and then she looks away and laughs at something Brooks didn't say.

blocks.name: KAPPA JUNIOR
blocks.text: Bookstore boy!
Brooks does look at Cal. Delighted, like he ordered him.
You came. You always come.
Careful. You spent your one.
Teddy says hi. He doesn't.
The absent-fathers guy. Still absent?
Then Tommy is in front of him, holding out the keg tap like the Olympic torch.
WHITAKER. KEG STAND. FOR THE TOAST.
WHITAKER. KEG STAND. FOR THE BUILDING.
The room hears it and turns. Forty faces swinging toward him at once, like the Kappa lawn on the first night. Somewhere behind him Brooks laughs his laugh, the one Cal knows from somewhere.

reaction.text: Four hockey players hoist him by the ankles like a trophy. The room chants WHI-TA-KER, WHI-TA-KER, the lawn all over again, his own name as a bass line. Eleven seconds upside down, beer up his nose, the bobcat watching.
When he comes up roaring, the room roaring with him, the blood in his head like surf, he sees Margaux on the stairs, watching. Exactly once. Then she isn't.
Brooks counted the seconds out loud, every one, in a clear voice, like a coach with a stopwatch at a pool. He's the first to clap.

You don't have to perform here.
I always have to perform.
Not with me.

Then, because they're idiots, they do Mrs. Okafor's grace in two-part harmony over a bag of tortilla chips, Dev on melody, Cal on a terrible tenor, "and bless my son's new friend, keep them both." Yusuf, against his will, against his religion, against everything he stands for, almost smiles. It's the best ten minutes of Cal's night, and nobody films it.

Hadley. You're in my light.
Brooks laughs, loud, head back, the laugh.
He's in everyone's light. It's his best quality.

Her eyes stay on Cal one beat too long. Two Kappas notice. Brooks notices them noticing, and his hand on the small of her back gets a little heavier, the way a hand does when it remembers what it's holding.

blocks.text: EXT. THE BARN, BACK PORCH. NIGHT (SAT 11:30 P.M.)
Simon left at 10:40, after a text that made him put his drink down. "A friend," he said, already in the coat. "A tall, sad friend." He didn't say which.

The back porch hangs over a dark yard full of dead lawn chairs and somebody's abandoned Zamboni-themed inflatable. Beyond the yard, past the last streetlight, there's a stripe of black that's darker than the sky. The lake. You can't see it so much as feel where the light stops.

Brooks is sitting on the porch rail with one foot up, the little leather notebook open on his knee and the golf pencil behind his ear, working the hockey boys like a scout at a combine. He asks one about his GPA, another about his father. He writes things down. They love it. Nobody has ever written anything down about them before.
Your father's in insurance? What kind? (writing) Good. Fire. Fire's good.
And you. You're from Duluth. Nobody's from Duluth. Say something in Duluth.

blocks.text: The goalie says "Ope," and the porch dies laughing, and Brooks writes it down like it's a stock tip. Cal watches him work and recognizes it, the way you recognize your own handwriting on a stranger's envelope: the questions that sound like compliments, the attention like a warm lamp, the way every boy on the porch now wants to be asked something next.
Then he turns to Tommy.
Reyes. Can you swim?
Like a Labrador. All heart, no form.
Brooks writes. It's longer than one word.
He told me "only toward money." Remember that.
Two-hundred free, he says. St. Anselm's. He says it like he's apologizing.
He told me he sinks like a stone.
Then he swam to my buoy like a fish. Whitaker knows the water. He'll teach you.
Whitaker doesn't swim for me. Maybe he'll swim for you.
Brooks doesn't look at the lake once. He looks at everything else on the porch, the chairs, the beer, the Zamboni, and never once at the stripe of black.
Your friend's fun, Whitaker. Bring him Thursday.

And Tommy lights up like a scoreboard. The Rho. The oldest house on Elm Row, senators and felons, wants him, a Worcester cop's kid on a hockey scholarship with one shower shoe. He looks at Cal like Cal just handed him the keys to something.
Out in the dark, the stripe of black lies there and doesn't say anything.

Look at you. Recruiting.
Cal feels, for one second, exactly like his father. A hand on a boy's shoulder, a door held open, a name on a list. He likes it. He likes it very much. And then, a second later, he doesn't.

Nobody drowns at the Rho.

His thumb goes to his left eyebrow. Then he laughs too, a half-second late, a little too loud, a man arriving at his own joke after it's started. He opens the notebook and writes something else down. Something short.

blocks.text: INT. THE BARN, UPSTAIRS BATHROOM. NIGHT (SUN 08-30, 1:10 A.M.)

An hour later Cal is looking for a bathroom that isn't occupied by a lacrosse player and a girl crying about her ex into the lacrosse player's jersey. He tries the last door at the end of the upstairs hall. It opens onto dark.
Tommy is sitting on the edge of the tub with the light off, heels of both hands pressed into his eyes, hard, like he's trying to push them back into his skull.
Shut it. Light's loud.
Cal shuts it. The dark is total except for a nightlight shaped like a shell, plugged in low by the sink.
You asked me that on the stairs. Don't make it a thing.
Here to decide for me again?

Tommy's phone is face-up on the tile by his foot. It buzzes. The screen lights the whole bathroom blue and Tommy flinches from it like it's a slap. DAD. He declines it without looking, by feel. Then he picks it up and types one-thumbed to someone saved as MA.

His voice goes flat and Worcester, all the highlight-reel bounce gone out of it.
Your name's on a building. Mine's on a roster. In pencil.

You're a good liar.
The best.
It's the first thing all night Cal's been proud of, and he shouldn't be.

blocks.text: INT. MARLOWE THEATER, REHEARSAL ROOM B. NIGHT (SAT 7:50 P.M.)

A black-box rehearsal room in the basement of the Marlowe: taped marks on a scuffed floor, a folding table with three chairs and a box of tissues, a radiator older than Gerald that clanks like it's auditioning too. Six girls in the hallway outside, all mouthing the same Russian.
At the door, MAE SATO, 19, sophomore stage manager: headset around her neck, clipboard, all black, a pencil in her bun, a deadpan so complete it loops all the way back around to funny.
You're the reader? You're not on my list.
He's my emergency contact.
This isn't an emergency. It's Chekhov.
She writes him in anyway, pencil already moving. "Name?"
Cal Pruitt.
It's the name on the license in his wallet. It comes out of his mouth like a reflex, like a sneeze.
Cal Pruitt. Rest in peace.
Sure.
She doesn't even look up. From a Bluetooth speaker on the table, her preshow playlist is playing "Seagull" by Bad Company.
It's a joke for no one. I make one a day. It keeps me alive.

Priya is vibrating. Her pupils are huge, black almost to the rim. She's talking fast, faster than the TV, about Stanislavski and her shoes and a dream she had about Varga's dog. She hasn't eaten. He watched her not eat on the walk over, a granola bar unwrapped and rewrapped twice and put back in her tote.
He's never been in love. It's his whole thing.
Great. Neither has Konstantin. He shoots himself.

Inside, at the folding table, PROF. LISE VARGA, the director, silver bob, a scarf that has seen Moscow, a cup of tea she isn't drinking. The scene is Act Four. Nina comes back to Konstantin after two years, wrecked and radiant, in the rain. She's been ruined by the man she ran away with and by the stage she ran away to, and she still loves both of them, and she has come back to tell the boy who loved her that she's going.
Priya stands on her mark. She closes her eyes. She opens them.
I'm a seagull. No. That's not it.

blocks.name: VARGA
blocks.text: Whenever you're ready.
Cal looks down at the pages in his hands. He has never acted in his life. He has also never done anything else.

choices.label: Play it for real.

reaction.text: He reads Konstantin like a man who has waited by a door, because he has, and like a man who has stood on the other side of one and not opened it, because he has done that too.

The room goes quiet. Mae stops writing. The radiator stops clanking, which it has never done for anyone. Opposite him, Priya rises to it, rises past it, and for six minutes she's better than anyone in the building, better than anyone he's ever seen in a room.

reaction.name: VARGA
reaction.text: Who ARE you?
Cal Pruitt.

reaction.name: VARGA
reaction.text: No. You're not.

reaction.text: He hams Konstantin like a Victorian ghost in a community-theater haunted house. He clutches his heart. He swoons into the radiator. He says "Nina" like it has six syllables.

Priya cracks. She laughs, a real laugh, her whole body letting go of whatever it's been holding since breakfast. And then, with the nerves gone, she turns and plays Nina straight, alone and devastating, to the empty corner of the room, while he stands there holding his pages like furniture with a script.

reaction.name: VARGA
reaction.text: Reader, thank you. Stop helping.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, DEV'S DOUBLE. NIGHT (MON 11:20 P.M.)

Cal came over to return a highlighter (green, the secret color) and to not be alone in his room with his father's blazer. Dev is already asleep in the crooked loft, earplugs in, wearing a sleep mask that says DOCTOR in pink glitter, a gift from his sister Ada, who believes in manifesting.

Yusuf is on the bottom bunk, hood up, laptop open, the screen light making a little blue room inside the dark one. He doesn't look up. He talks. He talks more than Cal has heard him talk in a week, which is to say about eleven words over budget, and every one of them lands.
The account schedules its posts. Seven-oh-four. Three-oh-seven. Seven-oh-four. Same app. Same device fingerprint. Posting IP is Lowell wifi. Third-floor access point.
He turns the laptop a few degrees, so Cal can see a graph of dots, like a constellation of bad nights.

Cal sits down on the floor with his back against the mini-fridge, the same spot as Friday, the hum against his spine. On the screen the dots make a pattern he doesn't want to recognize: most of them clustered between one and four in the morning, the hours when the third floor is supposed to be asleep and one door on it never is.
The stairwell photo was taken from a doorway on this floor. Low. Somebody sitting down, or short, or kneeling.
How do you even know all this?
Secret lottery.

He takes the Pruitt stairs two at a time, then three, and arrives in her doorway out of breath, like a man in a movie arriving at an airport gate, except it's an English professor's office and she isn't leaving and the fern is still dead.

blocks.name: MARSH
blocks.text: You came back. I'd have bet against it. I'm rarely wrong. Enjoy it; it won't happen often.
Marsh doesn't look up from the stack of essays in front of her, red pen moving.

blocks.name: MARSH

She holds out a sheet of paper without looking, and he takes it. PARTNER DRAFTS DUE WEDNESDAY.
Then she slides his essay out from under the stapler and holds that out too, still without looking. "Take it. Partners swap. I'm told that's the point of partners."

Is that it? I ran up three flights.

blocks.name: MARSH

blocks.name: MARSH
blocks.text: Everyone says that in September. It's the most reliable lie in the building.

The kettle is on. The fern is still dead. On the windowsill, beside it, there's a second mug now, clean, upside down on a paper towel, as if someone set it out this morning for a visitor she wasn't sure would come. He doesn't ask. She doesn't offer. Outside, the lake has gone the color of pewter, and a single rowing shell is crossing it, eight backs bending at once.
He's still in the blazer. Marsh's eyes go to the crest on the pocket and stay there one second too long, and she says nothing about it at all, and goes back to her red pen.
His phone buzzes in his hand. DAD.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, STAIRWELL. EVENING (TUE 6:40 P.M.)

Dev's second Whitlock Tuesday. Cal is on the third-floor landing, sitting on the top step with his phone, when Dev comes out of the double. Khakis. Brown church shoes, polished. Earbuds in. A white envelope in his back pocket, the corner showing.
Going for a run.

He doesn't look like a man going for a run. He looks like a man going to his own job interview, or to a funeral for someone he liked. His hair is brushed. He has a pen in his shirt pocket. He smells, faintly, of the good cologne, the one he saves.

Last Tuesday he said it and kept walking. This time he stops on the landing below and turns around and looks up at Cal, one hand on the banister, the stairwell light making a halo of nothing around his head.
You told me about your dad on that floor. The first night. I'll tell you this one day. Not today.
You'll tell me about your dad one day. I'll tell you this. Not today.
You told me the true thing yesterday. In front of everybody. I owe you one. Just not tonight.
He takes the envelope out of his pocket and holds it up between two fingers, like a ticket, like a boarding pass to somewhere.
Okay?
The church shoes. The envelope. Six-forty, again, exactly.
Nine months, his mother said at Dot's. God is good.
His best friend is asking him, in so many words, not to ask.

reaction.text: Dev smiles, and it's the nice smile, the one with something under it, the one that holds up a whole person like a beam.
Somewhere that keeps me nice.
He taps the banister and goes. Cal hears the front door, two floors down, then nothing, then the Quad.

choices.label: “Okay. Have a good run.”

reaction.text: Always do.
Dev taps the banister twice, like knocking on wood, and goes down the stairs two at a time in his church shoes.
It's the first promise Cal has kept all week that cost him something, and nobody will ever know he kept it, and that turns out to be the point.

reaction.text: Okay. Have a good run.
He says it so well. He says it exactly the way the good version of him would say it, and Dev believes him, because Dev believes him about almost everything, which is the whole problem with Dev.

blocks.text: EXT. MILL STREET. EVENING (TUE 6:52 P.M.)

Half a block back. Down the hill into town, the light going amber, then blue. Past Dot's, the pie case turning in the window like a slow jewelry box. Past the laundromat with its rows of turning windows. Past the tattoo parlor and its neon swallow, which buzzes like a fly against glass. Dev walks fast with his head down, the envelope back in his pocket, earbuds in, a man late for something he's never once been late for.
Somebody falls into step beside Cal, out of nowhere, hood up. Yusuf.
This is a bad idea.
I know.
I'm coming so it's a worse one.
Cal doesn't ask how long Yusuf has been watching the stairwell. He doesn't want to know the answer.

At the Anchor, the neon anchor and the hand-painted sign, EST. 1993, Dev slows. He doesn't go in. He raises a hand to the front window, flat, the way you'd say hi to someone on a train. Behind the bar, a big gray-haired man in a flannel lifts a dish towel back. Just that. Like they've done it before. Like it's a thing they do.
Then Dev turns uphill, away from campus, toward the white steeples. The streetlights come on in a row ahead of him, one after another, like they've been waiting for him specifically.
Cal stops at the corner. Yusuf stops with him.
Whatever it is, he'll tell you. Or he won't. Both are his.

Cal watches Dev's back go up the hill, smaller and smaller, the khakis, the church shoes, the way someone on the third floor has been watching his back go down the stairs at one in the morning with a phone held low.
I know what it's like to be followed.

Yusuf doesn't answer that. They turn around together and walk back up to campus without talking, past the swallow and the laundromat and Dot's, all the way up the hill. Dev never knows they were there. Yusuf will remember that Cal turned around.
INT. PRUITT HALL BASEMENT, THE WHITLOCK HERALD. NIGHT (TUE 8:30 P.M.)
Nora's text came at seven, as a single line, like a subpoena.

msgs.text: Herald. 8:30. Partners. Bring your draft or your excuses.

blocks.text: Two Herald staffers are leaving as he comes in, a boy with a camera and a girl with a stack of page proofs, and they both look at him the way you'd look at a headline that walked in on its own legs. "That's him," the girl says, not quietly. "The problem." The door shuts behind them.
I'm a problem now. Officially. In print.
You were always a problem. Now you're a well-sourced one.

He arrived ten minutes late, with Mill Street still in his face. Nora looks up from her screen and looks at him for exactly as long as it takes. "You look like you followed someone." He doesn't say anything. She doesn't push. She files it.

The Herald is a basement under Pruitt that has been a newsroom since 1919 and smells like it: steam pipes along the ceiling that tick and hiss, framed front pages going back a century (ARMISTICE, MOON, the Whitaker Commons groundbreaking in 1994), a row of ankle-height windows at the top of the wall full of passing shoes. At the back, the editor-in-chief's door, shut, a line of light under it, a sound of someone typing like they're angry at the keys.
Nora's corner is a desk with three coffee rings on it in a perfect Olympic overlap, and a corkboard the size of a door, covered entirely by a flowered bedsheet, thumbtacked at all four corners.

One corner of the sheet has slipped. Under it, pinned flat, there's a printout of a typed list he recognizes, the faintly uneven letters, the alphabet with a hole in it. His homework. Nora pulls the corner straight without comment and pushes the thumbtack in with her whole thumb.
Simon says it's the most-read thing the Herald's run since the moon landing.
Simon says a lot of things. Sit. Don't touch the pipes, they're older than your grandfather's money and angrier.
He sits on an overturned milk crate stenciled PROPERTY OF THE WHITLOCK HERALD 1971 and looks at the bedsheet, and looks away from the bedsheet, and Nora watches him do both.
She hands him a cold brew. Black. Large.
Even.
Your first lie. "We're ok." Was it?
"No comment," he says. In a room full of reporters.
She glances at his hand before she says anything, like checking a dog before you pet it.
Marsh says partners swap placement essays. I'm not swapping. Mine's about a room I'm not done leaving.
He reads her the way he reads everyone, and for once it works, a little. She's protecting something. Not someone. Something with edges.
She sees him reading her.
Eyes up, Whitlock.

choices.label: Hand her his essay anyway.

reaction.text: He takes the folded pages out of his jacket and puts them on her desk, on the coffee rings, and doesn't say anything about them. She looks at them for a long time before she touches them.

Then she reads it, under the ticking pipes, with her coffee going cold. All of it. The drive north in March. The lobster rolls at two in the morning. The fish kite off the hood of the car. The ice machine. The phone pulled under the bathroom door by its cord. He watches her not react, page after page. It's a skill. He recognizes it. He has it.
When she's done she folds it once along the old fold and slides it back.
Okay.
She doesn't make it a story. She doesn't say anything about the motel post, or the account, or the comments.
That's somebody's life. It's yours.
She takes a pen and draws a line through something on a list taped to the side of her monitor. He realizes, too late to say anything, that it's his coffee debt. She's been keeping a ledger.

choices.label: Show her the cleaners ticket: “Weird thing in my dad's blazer.”

reaction.text: He slides it out of his wallet, the yellowed little ticket with the rusted pinhole, and puts it on her desk under the lamp. "Weird thing in my dad's blazer. The Rho one. Lake water. Who gets lake water on a blazer?"
Nora reads it. She reads it again.

She goes absolutely still. Not reporter-still. The other kind. The stillness from the check-in tent on the very first day, when he read her notebook upside down. It lasts too long. The pipes tick through it.
Can I take a picture of this?
Sure. Why?
For nothing. It's a weird thing. I like weird things.

She photographs it twice, the front and then the front again, and gives it back to him, and her hand is shaking, a small fast tremor like a phone on vibrate, and she puts the hand flat on the desk to stop it, and she does not tell him why.

choices.label: Nod at the bedsheet: “What's under there?”

reaction.text: Eyes up, Whitlock.
She says it automatically, the way you say bless you. Then, quieter, not looking at him, looking at the sheet:
It's a story I'm not ready to tell. Like yours.
She reaches up and pulls one thumbtack tighter, the top left, pressing it until her thumbnail goes white.

It's the most she's ever given him. They both know it. Neither of them says so. The pipes tick, and somebody's shoes go by the window at ankle height, and the sheet hangs there like a ghost in a children's play, waiting for its line.

blocks.text: INT. SIGMA KAPPA RHO HOUSE, THE CHAPTER ROOM. NIGHT (TUE 9:00 P.M.)
Brooks's text came at seven.

msgs.text: Econ 110. Welcome to the boys who matter.
Chapter room, 9. Bring the blazer. Pre-rush quiz.

blocks.text: Which is against every rule the Interfraternity Council has ever written, so it's called a dinner, and there's no dinner.
He arrives late, with the hill still in his legs. Brooks, at the door, looks down at his shoes, at the town grit on them, and smiles. "Slumming?"

The chapter room again: the long table, the candles, the founders on the wall in their 1890 frock coats looking down like disappointed uncles, the silver loving cup in the center gone dark at the handles. The legacy freshmen from Thursday's dinner, in their fathers' blazers, sleeves too long or too short, shoulders that belong to other decades. Teddy Pemberton's is two sizes too big. He keeps pushing the sleeves up. They keep coming back down over his hands, like his father's still in there, reaching for something.

Cal has his on a hanger, over his shoulder, like a garment bag. Brooks stops him at the door with two fingers on his chest. "On. In front of everybody." Cal puts it on in front of everybody. It fits. The room goes a little quiet at how well.
Cal is wearing his. He's been wearing it since yesterday.
Cal is wearing his.
Brooks sees it and stops. Actually stops, in the middle of a sentence to Fitz, the way a man stops at the top of a staircase in the dark.
That's his. From that year.
Then the smile comes back on like a porch light.
You spent your one at dinner, Whitaker. Let's see you earn another.

The quiz. Each legacy stands and recites his father's pledge class, alphabetically, the way you'd recite the begats. Fitz keeps score on a cocktail napkin in a pink tie. Lindgren gets through his with one stumble. Teddy gets his father's year wrong, all of it, the wrong class, and the room pretends it didn't hear, which is the kindest and cruelest thing Cal has seen a room do.
Then Cal. He's word-perfect without even trying. Dev's flashcards are still in his head, in Dev's voice.
You asked me in writing. Ask me to my face.
Then Cal. He knows it cold. He recites it, and the whole time he can feel the photo he sent sitting in Nora's phone, like a stone in a shoe.
You know the water. You know the class. You're almost done.
You don't know the water yet. You will.
You don't know the water yet. You will.
You don't know the water yet. You will.
Brooks walks him down the list himself, name by name, standing at his shoulder. Abernathy. Brandt. Carver. And stops at the dash.
And this one?
You tell me.
Brooks leans in. The candlelight does something to his face, makes it older, makes it look like a face Cal has seen in an oval on a wall.
A boy who couldn't swim.
And then the laugh, the one Cal knows from somewhere, the one he's been hearing his whole life from the other side of closed doors.
Joking. Transferred. Something boring.
His thumb goes to his left eyebrow.

reaction.text: He takes it out of his wallet and lays it on the table next to the loving cup, under the candles. "Found it in his pocket. Lake water. You'd think they'd have gotten it out."
Brooks picks it up. Reads it. And for one second all the color leaves his face, all of it at once, like someone pulled a plug.
Can I keep this?
It's a dry-cleaning ticket, Hadley. Frame it.

Brooks folds it into his own wallet, carefully, along no fold it had before, like a pressed flower, and laughs at nothing for the rest of the night. He laughs at Fitz's jokes. He laughs at Teddy. He laughs at the founders. Every laugh a little early.
INT. SIGMA KAPPA RHO HOUSE, BROOKS'S ROOM. NIGHT (WED 1:20 A.M.)

Every light on. Brooks at his desk. He opens the drawer and lifts out the old leather book stamped 1991. He opens it, for the first time we've seen, to a page we never see. He lays the cleaners ticket inside it, flat, the way you press a leaf. He closes it. Four in. Hold. Eight out.

choices.label: “Was he in my father's pledge class?”

reaction.text: Was he in my father's pledge class? The dash. Was he one of his?
Brooks leans across the candles, so close Cal can smell the Stoli and the cedar.
Ask your father.
A smile.
I dare you.

The other legacies laugh, because they think it's hazing, because everything in this room is hazing. Teddy laughs loudest, from inside his sleeves. Cal doesn't laugh. And Brooks sees him not laugh, and something in his face goes careful, the way a man goes careful on ice.

choices.label: Recite the whole list perfectly, dash and all.

reaction.text: He stands. He recites it. All nineteen pledges, in order, in his father's voice, which he didn't know he could do. "Abernathy, John. Brandt, Kurt. Carver, Paul." A breath. "Dash." A breath. "Cohen, David."
The room laughs at "dash." Somebody bangs the table. Brooks doesn't laugh.
Perfect. Like him.

Fitz writes WHITAKER · 100 on the napkin and holds it up like a scorecard at the Olympics. Cal has won a quiz he didn't want to take, about a year he wasn't alive for, and he feels sick in a way he can't place, somewhere low and cold, like swallowed lake.

blocks.text: INT. PRUITT HALL, MARSH'S OFFICE. NIGHT (TUE 11:40 P.M.)
The building is empty. One lamp on Marsh's desk, green-shaded, and outside her window the lake is black all the way across, no line between water and sky, as if the window has been painted over.

Marsh sits with a plain white card in front of her and a fountain pen, an old one, the kind you have to fill. She doesn't grade anything. She writes slowly, in the row of small knives, and the card fills line by line.
"He's here."
"He signed his own name."
"He stayed."
"He ran. They run first."
"He'll slide it under the door. I'd bet my life."

She blots it. She reads it once. She seals it in an envelope and writes an address on the front that we never see, the pen hiding it, then her hand. She props it against her bag by the door for the morning post. Behind her the shelves are a soft blur of spines, nothing legible, a thousand books with their mouths shut. She turns off the lamp and sits there a while longer, in the dark, with the lake.
INT. CAL'S SINGLE, LOWELL HOUSE. NIGHT (WED 09-02, 3:07 A.M.)
Gerald bangs. Right on time, the only thing in Cal's life that is.
Cal is at the desk in the bay window in a T-shirt, his father's blazer on the back of the door behind him like someone waiting to be let in.
Cal is at the desk in the bay window in a T-shirt, his father's blazer finally off, hung over the back of the chair he's sitting in.
Cal is at the desk in the bay window in a T-shirt, his father's blazer over the back of the chair he's sitting in.
He's writing. Not on the legal pad. In the new Moleskine, the black one he started the first night, the one that's been empty for a week.
On its first page, at the top, in small letters, it says: For nobody.
We see the line in his hand, his pen still moving at the end of it.
I said, Dad, she's not sleeping.
He said, Where are you. I told him the name of the motel. I read it off the phone, off the little card by the bed, because I didn't know it. I didn't know where I was.
He keeps going.
On the corner of the desk, stuck to the lamp, a Post-it in purple marker from Saturday night, in Priya's handwriting: NINA SAYS THANK U. With a drawing of a seagull that looks like a duck.
His phone lights up on the desk. @lowell.three. A new post.

A photo of a window. His window. The bay window of the single on the third floor of Lowell House, lit gold in the dark, a figure bent at a desk inside it, small, taken from far below, from the black middle of the Quad. Caption: "3:07 a.m. the legacy's up writing his book. we live here too."

He looks down through the glass. The Quad is empty. The paths are empty. The steps of Whitaker Commons are empty under the floodlights, all the way up to his grandfather's name. Nobody. Nobody he can see.
He looks at the photo again. Somebody was out there. Somebody stood in the dark with their phone and watched him write.
He turns the phone face-down on the desk.
He keeps writing.
Across the hall, in the dark of the double, Yusuf's laptop chimes once. He sits up.
CUT TO BLACK.
